This workload accesses local memory (https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-c-programming-guide/index.html#device-memory-accesses), accounting for 1.13% of all sectors requested in L1TEX. Local memory refers to a memory space that is private to each thread. Although it is logically distinct, local memory resides in global memory. This can lead to higher memory latency compared to the usage of registers or shared memory, a decrease in available bandwidth to global memory, and an increase in executed instructions.
All of the local memory accesses are due to register spilling (https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-c-programming-guide/index.html#variable-memory-space-specifiers). 8.26% of all local loads and 79.17% of all local stores spill into the L2 cache, accounting for 0.10% of all sectors requested in L2.

For more advice on how to reduce the usage of local memory refer to the documentation (https://docs.nvidia.com/nsight-compute/ProfilingGuide/index.html#metrics-hw-memory)."

This workload accesses local memory (https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-c-programming-guide/index.html#device-memory-accesses), accounting for 4.91% of all sectors requested in L1TEX. Local memory refers to a memory space that is private to each thread. Although it is logically distinct, local memory resides in global memory. This can lead to higher memory latency compared to the usage of registers or shared memory, a decrease in available bandwidth to global memory, and an increase in executed instructions.
Some of the local memory accesses are due to register spilling (https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-c-programming-guide/index.html#variable-memory-space-specifiers), accounting for 52.72% of the local memory load (LDL) and 100.00% of the local store (STL) instructions. 21.97% of all local loads and 88.46% of all local stores spill into the L2 cache, accounting for 0.14% of all sectors requested in L2.
One common reason for the use of local memory is arrays being too large to fit into registers or not being indexed using compile time constants (see the Local Memory" section of the CUDA Programming Guide (https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-c-programming-guide/index.html#device-memory-accesses). For more advice on how to reduce the usage of local memory refer to the documentation (https://docs.nvidia.com/nsight-compute/ProfilingGuide/index.html#metrics-hw-memory)."

Every scheduler is capable of issuing one instruction per cycle, but for this workload each scheduler only issues an instruction every 2.4 cycles. This might leave hardware resources underutilized and may lead to less optimal performance. Out of the maximum of 16 warps per scheduler, this workload allocates an average of 2.99 active warps per scheduler, but only an average of 0.55 warps were eligible per cycle. Eligible warps are the subset of active warps that are ready to issue their next instruction. Every cycle with no eligible warp results in no instruction being issued and the issue slot remains unused. To increase the number of eligible warps, avoid possible load imbalances due to highly different execution durations per warp.
